notes: An Update to the Budget and Economic Outlook: 2024 to 2034 (June 2024 CBO baseline). CBO data publication: 10-year budget projections (https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51118) and economic projections (https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51135).

Fiscal years run October to September and are named by the calendar year in which they end. FY2023 is the actual year in this baseline; later years are CBO baseline projections under current law, not a forecast of policy.

The deficit is the total (unified) federal deficit; positive values are deficits. Debt is debt held by the public at the end of the fiscal year. Net interest is net interest outlays. The primary balance is net interest minus the deficit, as a share of GDP.
GDP is fiscal-year nominal GDP implied by CBO's published debt-to-GDP ratio. Other ratios are calculated from dollar amounts and that GDP, and match CBO's published ratios where both exist.

Economic assumptions are fiscal-year averages from CBO's economic projections: real and nominal GDP growth, CPI-U and PCE inflation, the unemployment rate, the federal funds rate, the 3-month Treasury bill rate, the 10-year Treasury note yield, private-wage growth (employment cost index) and CBO's output gap (% of potential GDP).

Structural (cyclically adjusted) deficit: CBO's deficit excluding automatic stabilizers (https://www.cbo.gov/publication/51139, November 2024 estimates, built on this baseline). Shares of GDP here use actual GDP; CBO also publishes them as shares of potential GDP.

rules.name: Statutory debt limit
rules.description: A cap set in law (31 U.S.C. 3101) on the total amount of debt the Treasury may issue, including debt held by the public and debt held by federal trust funds. It limits the financing of obligations already made; it does not limit spending or deficits themselves.
rules.definition: Applies to debt subject to limit, a measure that differs from debt held by the public (used elsewhere in this dashboard). Congress raises, suspends or redefines the limit by legislation.
rules.assessmentNote: Descriptive only: the limit is not a fiscal target and has no forecast headroom in CBO's baseline. The chart shows CBO's projection of debt subject to limit; the statutory dollar limit itself is not shown.

indicator.measure: Debt subject to limit, $ billions (February 2026 CBO baseline)

rules.name: Statutory Pay-As-You-Go (PAYGO)
rules.description: The Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010 (Title I of Public Law 111-139) requires that new mandatory spending and revenue legislation, taken together, not increase projected deficits; a net cost recorded on OMB's scorecards at the end of a congressional session triggers sequestration of certain mandatory programs.
rules.definition: A budget-enforcement procedure for new legislation, not a target for the deficit or debt. Congress can and does exclude legislation from the scorecards.
rules.assessmentNote: Descriptive only: no headroom or compliance verdict is computed.

notes: US federal government, unified budget (on-budget plus off-budget, including Social Security and the Postal Service); federal fiscal years run October to September and are named by the year in which they end (FY2026 ends September 2026). Three CBO baselines are shown (June 2024, January 2025 and February 2026); each new baseline is added alongside the earlier ones after review rather than replacing them.
CBO baselines are projections under current law (with CBO's conventions, e.g. discretionary funding grown with inflation); they are not forecasts of future legislation.
The United States has no numerical fiscal rules. The statutory debt limit and Statutory PAYGO are listed as descriptive budget constraints with no headroom or verdict.
History: CBO Historical Budget Data (February 2026), FY1962 to the latest actual year. Debt is debt held by the public; GDP is implied from CBO's published debt-to-GDP ratio.

Debt dynamics inputs (net interest, debt held by the public, nominal GDP growth, primary balance) come from one CBO vintage; the effective interest rate and debt-stabilizing primary balance are dashboard calculations. CBO also publishes its own average interest rate on debt held by the public.

The forecast bridge needs a net-investment split, which CBO does not publish, so it is not shown. CBO publishes no machine-readable borrowing sensitivities in its open-data repository, so none are shown.
